docs.title: go-pki-cmp
docs.text:
go-pki-cmp is a Go library for the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP). It has four packages:

  • pkicmp encodes, parses, protects and verifies CMP and CRMF messages
  • client enrolls, updates and revokes certificates and asks a CA for information
  • server serves the same operations to CMP clients as an http.Handler in front of your CA
  • cms encrypts and decrypts the CMS EnvelopedData and EncryptedValue that proof of possession by decryption needs

The server handles the protocol: transport, message protection, transactions, polling and certificate confirmation. Your application supplies issuance, credential lookup and authorization policy through Go interfaces. cmp-issuer, a cert-manager external issuer, is built on this library.

Certificates can carry post-quantum ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or composite ML-DSA keys and all of them can sign CMP messages. ML-KEM keys are certified through proof of possession by decryption. The support matrix lists what is covered.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp

The module needs Go 1.27.3 or newer. Releases up to v0.3.2 use the module path github.com/misiektoja/go-pkicmp-ng.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
A Client holds an endpoint and configuration only. Each Send* or Get* call runs one complete operation and keeps its transaction state, such as the transaction ID and nonces, for that call alone. One Client can therefore serve many goroutines.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Your code
    participant C as client.Client
    participant CA as CMP server
    App->>C: SendIR(key, creds)
    C->>CA: ir (protected with creds)
    CA-->>C: ip, or pollRep while the CA decides
    C->>C: verify protection, certReqId and issued key
    C->>CA: certConf
    CA-->>C: pkiConf
    C-->>App: EnrollResult

The call returns only after the whole exchange, including polling and confirmation. A context deadline bounds it. Enrollment and Response verification describe each step.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
server.NewCAServer wraps your CA in a handler, applies the policy middleware and returns a Server that implements http.Handler. server.New takes any Handler instead, for full control such as custom routing or a registration authority proxy.

Every request passes these stages in order:

  1. HTTP checks. Only POST with Content-Type: application/pkixcmp is accepted. Bodies are limited by server.MaxRequestBodySize, 1 MiB by default.
  2. Header checks. The protocol version must be 2 or 3 and a recipient the server does not answer to is refused.
  3. Protection. The MAC is checked with the secret from SecretLookup or the signature with the certificate from CertificateLookup. The result is a SenderIdentity.
  4. Transaction checks. Nonces, the transaction ID and the transaction limits are checked against the state of the sender's transaction.
  5. Policy middleware. LightweightPolicy and your own middleware accept or refuse the request.
  6. Built-in request checks. The handler that NewCAServer builds verifies proof of possession and decodes BasicConstraints for every certificate request, with or without a policy.
  7. Your CA. IssueCertificate, RevokeCertificate, CheckPending or a support message provider decides the answer.
  8. Response. The server protects the response with the MAC of a MAC-protected request or else with the WithSigner key. It then records the transaction state.
flowchart LR
    R[HTTP request] --> P[Verify protection]
    P --> T[Transaction state]
    T --> M[Policy middleware]
    M --> B[Proof of possession]
    B --> CA[Your CA]
    CA --> S[Protect response]

A refusal at any stage becomes a CMP error message or the rejection in an ip, cp, kup or rp where RFC 9810 asks for one. An error your code returns that is not a *server.Error becomes a bare systemFailure, so internal detail never reaches the peer.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
The server keys each transaction by the sender's verified credential and the transaction ID. One client cannot continue or hijack another client's transaction even with the same transaction ID. Transactions live in memory:

  • CleanupExpired removes completed and stale transactions and must be called periodically.
  • WithMaxTransactions and WithMaxTransactionsPerCredential cap the state a client can create.
  • SnapshotTransactions and RestoreTransactions move the state to durable storage or a new process.

Transactions and recovery describes each.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This page runs the example CA and client from the repository and explains what they exchange. Every piece of the example maps to a page of the client or server guide, so once it runs you know what to replace in your own code.

The example CA keeps everything in memory and signs with a throwaway self-signed root. The client enrolls a key with a shared secret, updates it with a signed request and revokes the result.

docs.text:
• Go 1.27.3 or newer, the minimum the module declares

git clone https://github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp.git
cd go-pki-cmp

docs.title: Step 1: start the CA
docs.text:
go run ./examples/mockserver/cmd

INFO CA ready subject="CN=Test CA" serial=240565888259335087214779031597002404039
INFO mockserver listening addr=localhost:8080 path=/cmp

The program creates the CA, registers one shared secret under the reference my-device and serves CMP on http://localhost:8080/cmp:

// Command mockserver is a minimal CMP server for testing.
package main

import (
    "crypto/x509"
    "log/slog"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"

    "github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp/examples/mockserver"
    "github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp/server"
)

func main() {
    // Create a logger for the server.
    log := slog.Default()

    // Create a CA with shared secrets for MAC-based enrollment.
    // Each entry maps a senderKID (reference number) to an Initial Authentication
    // Key (IAK). In production these would be loaded from a database or a
    // secrets manager.
    ca, err := mockserver.New(map[string][]byte{
        "my-device": []byte("test-shared-secret"),
    }, log)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("creating CA", "error", err)
        return
    }
    log.Info("CA ready", "subject", ca.Cert().Subject.String(), "serial", ca.Cert().SerialNumber)

    // Connect the CA into a CMP server.
    //
    //   - LightweightPolicy: enforces the mandatory checks from RFC 9483.
    //   - WithSigner: signs every outgoing response with the CA key; a crypto.Signer
    //     so an HSM-backed signer can be used in production.
    //   - WithExtraCerts: appends the CA cert to outgoing response extraCerts.
    //   - WithSecretLookup: enables MAC (shared-secret) protection for IR/CR.
    //   - WithCertificateLookup: enables signature protection for KUR/certConf/RR.
    //   - CentralKeyGeneration: lets a client ask the CA to generate its key pair.
    //   - WithRAAuthorizer: accepts requests that a registration authority with
    //     an id-kp-cmcRA certificate from this CA forwards in nested messages.
    srv := server.NewCAServer(ca,
        server.LightweightPolicy(),
        server.WithSigner(ca.Key(), ca.Cert()),
        server.WithExtraCerts([]*x509.Certificate{ca.Cert()}),
        server.WithSecretLookup(ca),
        server.WithCertificateLookup(ca),
        ca.CentralKeyGeneration(),
        server.WithRAAuthorizer(ca),
    )
    if err := srv.Err(); err != nil {
        log.Error("server misconfigured", "err", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    // Periodically remove stale transactions from clients that never send certConf.
    // A transaction is stale once the confirm wait time has passed, 10 seconds
    // unless the server is built with WithConfirmWaitTime.
    go func() {
        for range time.Tick(30 * time.Second) {
            srv.CleanupExpired()
        }
    }()

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("/cmp", srv)

    log.Info("mockserver listening", "addr", "localhost:8080", "path", "/cmp")
    httpSrv := &http.Server{
        Addr:         "localhost:8080",
        Handler:      mux,
        ReadTimeout:  30 * time.Second,
        WriteTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
        IdleTimeout:  120 * time.Second,
    }
    if err := httpSrv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil {
        log.Error("server error", "error", err)
    }
}

mockserver.MockCA implements the CA side: issuance, revocation, the shared secret and certificate lookups and the support messages. Its source is in examples/mockserver.

INFO sending IR with MAC protection
INFO enrolled subject="CN=my-device" issuer="CN=Test CA" serial=322200269625980906720798033765771843406
INFO received CA subject="CN=Test CA" issuer="CN=Test CA" serial=240565888259335087214779031597002404039
INFO certificate verified
INFO sending KUR with signature protection
INFO renewed subject="CN=my-device" issuer="CN=Test CA" serial=296525914232565556297304034835094423049
INFO certificate verified
INFO sending RR with signature protection
INFO certificate revoked serial=296525914232565556297304034835094423049

The client runs three operations in turn:

// Command mockclient is a minimal CMP client for testing.
package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/ecdsa"
    "crypto/elliptic"
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/x509"
    "crypto/x509/pkix"
    "log/slog"

    "github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp/client"
    "github.com/misiektoja/go-pki-cmp/pkicmp"
)

func printCert(log *slog.Logger, label string, cert *x509.Certificate) {
    log.Info(label,
        "subject", cert.Subject.String(),
        "issuer", cert.Issuer.String(),
        "serial", cert.SerialNumber.String(),
    )
}

func verifyCert(log *slog.Logger, cert *x509.Certificate, trustedCAs *x509.CertPool) {
    if _, err := cert.Verify(x509.VerifyOptions{Roots: trustedCAs}); err != nil {
        log.Error("certificate verification failed", "error", err)
        return
    }
    log.Info("certificate verified")
}

func main() {
    log := slog.Default()

    endpoint := "http://localhost:8080/cmp"
    subject := pkix.Name{CommonName: "my-device"}

    // --- Step 1: Initial enrollment (IR) with MAC protection ---
    //
    // A new device has no certificate yet. It authenticates using a pre-shared
    // secret (Initial Authentication Key) and a reference number (senderKID)
    // that tells the server which secret to look up.

    // Generate a key pair for the certificate we're requesting.
    key, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("generating key", "error", err)
        return
    }

    // Create MAC credentials from the shared secret.
    creds, err := pkicmp.NewMACCredentials([]byte("test-shared-secret"))
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("creating credentials", "error", err)
        return
    }

    // Send the IR request.
    c := client.NewClient(endpoint)

    log.Info("sending IR with MAC protection")
    result, err := c.SendIR(context.Background(), key, creds,
        client.WithSenderKID([]byte("my-device")), // reference number for the shared secret
        client.WithSender(subject),                // sender DN in PKIHeader
        client.WithTemplateSubject(subject),       // requested certificate subject
    )
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("IR failed", "error", err)
        return
    }

    printCert(log, "enrolled", result.Certificate)

    // The IR response includes CA certificates in caPubs for trust bootstrap.
    // We use them to verify the enrolled certificate and as trust anchors for
    // the server's signature-protected KUR response later.
    trustedCAs := x509.NewCertPool()
    for _, ca := range result.CAPubs {
        printCert(log, "received CA", ca)
        trustedCAs.AddCert(ca)
    }
    verifyCert(log, result.Certificate, trustedCAs)

    // --- Step 2: Key update (KUR) with signature protection ---
    //
    // The device now has a certificate. It proves its identity by signing the
    // request with the existing key, and sends the CA chain in extraCerts so
    // the server can verify the sender's certificate.

    // Generate a new key for the renewed certificate.
    newKey, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("generating new key", "error", err)
        return
    }

    // Create signature credentials: the old key signs the request, the old
    // certificate identifies the sender, and the CA chain enables the server
    // to verify the sender's certificate.
    sigCreds, err := pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(key, result.Certificate, result.CAPubs...)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("creating signature credentials", "error", err)
        return
    }

    // For KUR, configure trust anchors so the client can verify the server's
    // signature-protected response.
    c = client.NewClient(endpoint, client.WithTrustedCAs(trustedCAs))

    log.Info("sending KUR with signature protection")
    renewal, err := c.SendKUR(context.Background(), newKey, sigCreds,
        client.WithSender(subject),
        client.WithTemplateSubject(subject),
    )
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("KUR failed", "error", err)
        return
    }

    printCert(log, "renewed", renewal.Certificate)
    verifyCert(log, renewal.Certificate, trustedCAs)

    // --- Step 3: Revocation (RR) with signature protection ---
    //
    // The device retires the renewed certificate. RFC 9483 §4.2 expects the
    // request to be signed with the certificate being revoked, which proves
    // the device is entitled to revoke it.
    revCreds, err := pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(newKey, renewal.Certificate, result.CAPubs...)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("creating revocation credentials", "error", err)
        return
    }

    log.Info("sending RR with signature protection")
    err = c.SendRR(context.Background(), renewal.Certificate, pkicmp.CRLReasonCessationOfOperation, revCreds)
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("RR failed", "error", err)
        return
    }
    log.Info("certificate revoked", "serial", renewal.Certificate.SerialNumber.String())
}

docs.title: What happens behind the scenes
docs.text:
1. Initial enrollment. The client sends an ir protected with a MAC derived from the shared secret. senderKID carries my-device, so the server finds the secret through LookupSecret. The server verifies the MAC and the proof of possession, builds a certificate template from the request and calls IssueCertificate. The ip carries the certificate and the CA certificate in caPubs. The client confirms the certificate with certConf and the server answers pkiConf.
  2. Key update. The client signs a kur with the certificate from step 1. The server finds that certificate through LookupCertificate, verifies the signature and issues a certificate for the new key. The client verifies the signed kup against the CA certificate it received in step 1.
  3. Revocation. The client sends an rr signed with the certificate it revokes. The server checks that the signer is that certificate and calls RevokeCertificate. The rp reports acceptance.

The server log shows each lookup, issuance, confirmation and revocation.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text: Behavior to plan around in the current release. Each item states what is missing and what it means for your application.

docs.title: Some CMP operations are not implemented
docs.text: Key recovery, cross-certification and announcements are not implemented. Requests for them are refused with badRequest and the text "message type not supported".

docs.title: One request per nested message
docs.text: A registration authority may forward one request per nested message. Batches (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.2) are refused with badRequest. A client with WithRegistrationAuthority sends one request per nested message and does not batch.

docs.title: Central key generation needs a key that can decrypt
docs.text: A centrally generated private key is encrypted for the requester. A signature-protected request needs an RSA or ECDSA P-256, P-384 or P-521 protection key. Other keys, such as Ed25519 or ML-DSA, can receive a generated key only through a MAC-protected request. The CMP version 2 EncryptedValue form of the private key is not supported.

docs.title: ML-KEM-512 and older Dilithium encodings
docs.text: ML-KEM-512 keys are refused because the Go standard library does not implement them. Only the final ML-DSA encodings are supported, not the older Dilithium ones.

docs.title: Composite ML-DSA and SLH-DSA chains
docs.text: crypto/x509 cannot check composite ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signatures, so the library verifies such paths itself. A certificate signed with a composite or SLH-DSA key is accepted only when its issuer certificate travels in the message, in extraCerts or caPubs, even if that issuer is a trust anchor. No certificate in such a path may carry name constraints.

docs.title: SLH-DSA CAs sign slowly
docs.text: An SLH-DSA CA key signs every issued certificate and, as the WithSigner key, every protected response. The small parameter sets, whose names end in s, can take hundreds of milliseconds or more per signature. An enrollment with explicit confirmation needs at least two signatures. A separate classical or ML-DSA signer certificate in WithSigner keeps the responses fast. Errors the server returns before authentication are signed too, so every unauthenticated request costs a signature unless WithUnprotectedErrorsBeforeAuthentication leaves those errors unprotected.

docs.title: Proof by decryption needs a capable CA
docs.text: The client can enroll a key that cannot sign only at a CA that supports the encrypted certificate or challenge-response method. RFC 9483 lets a CA refuse both for keys that can sign. X25519 keys are refused by the server.

docs.title: State lives in memory
docs.text: Transactions, waiting requests and challenges live in the Server. Replicas share them only through SnapshotTransactions and RestoreTransactions, which your application must call while it excludes concurrent requests. See Transactions and recovery.

docs.title: No response cache
docs.text: A client that retries an exact request after a lost response starts a new operation, which may issue a second certificate. Keep a response cache when that matters.

docs.title: Subjects lose attributes without WithRawSubject
docs.text: The template subject is rebuilt from pkix.Name, which drops types such as domainComponent and emailAddress and may reorder the rest. WithRawSubject keeps the requested encoding.

docs.title: crypto/x509 cannot certify every key
docs.text: Composite ML-DSA keys need compositex509.CreateCertificate. ML-KEM and SLH-DSA subject keys need a signer outside crypto/x509, and so does a CA whose own key is SLH-DSA.

docs.title: No built-in rate limits
docs.text: The server caps transactions in total and per credential. Other limits belong in your middleware.

docs.title: Polling time is chosen by the CA
docs.text: The client waits as long as the CA asks, within WithCheckAfterLimits, up to WithMaxPolls times. Only a context deadline bounds the whole operation. WithDeferredPolling returns at the first waiting answer, so that ResumeEnrollment can collect the certificate later.

docs.text: Mechanism Algorithms MAC PBMAC1 (default) and PasswordBasedMac with HMAC-SHA1 to HMAC-SHA512. Iteration counts from 100 to 1000000 are accepted by default Signature RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 and ECDSA with SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, Ed25519, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87, SLH-DSA and composite ML-DSA SHA-1 signatures RSA and ECDSA with SHA-1, off by default. WithSHA1Signatures in the client or server package accepts them

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text: Capability Status Key recovery, cross-certification and announcements Not implemented A centrally generated private key in EncryptedValue Refused by the client and never sent by the server Several requests in one nested message (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.2) Refused with badRequest and never sent by the client ML-KEM-512 Refused, the Go standard library does not implement it Older Dilithium encodings Not supported HashSLH-DSA, the pre-hash variant of SLH-DSA Refused SHAKE256 as the hashAlg of a certificate confirmation Refused. An explicit hashAlg may be SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 X25519 keys for proof by decryption Refused with badAlg RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 key transport in EnvelopedData Refused Protocol versions other than 2 and 3, such as pvno 0 or 1 Refused with unsupportedVersion

docs.title: Keys the CA generates
docs.text:
A device that cannot generate a good key pair itself can ask the CA to do it (RFC 9483 section 4.1.6). SendIRWithCentralKeyGeneration, SendCRWithCentralKeyGeneration and SendKURWithCentralKeyGeneration send a request without a public key and return the private key with the certificate:

// nil leaves the key algorithm to the CA.
result, err := c.SendIRWithCentralKeyGeneration(context.Background(), nil, creds,
    client.WithSenderKID([]byte("my-device")),
    client.WithTemplateSubject(pkix.Name{CommonName: "my-device"}),
)
key := result.GeneratedKey.PrivateKey

To ask for a key algorithm, pass its AlgorithmIdentifier. An elliptic curve key names its curve in the parameters:

curve, _ := asn1.Marshal(asn1.ObjectIdentifier{1, 3, 132, 0, 34}) // P-384
algorithm := &pkicmp.AlgorithmIdentifier{
    Algorithm:  asn1.ObjectIdentifier{1, 2, 840, 10045, 2, 1}, // id-ecPublicKey
    Parameters: curve,
}

The CA decides which algorithms it generates and refuses others, usually with badAlg.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
The CA encrypts the private key for the requester, so the credentials of the request must be able to decrypt it:

Credentials Encryption pkicmp.MACCredentials To the shared secret (RFC 5652 section 6.2.4) pkicmp.SignatureCredentials with an RSA key Key transport to the protection key pkicmp.SignatureCredentials with an ECDSA key on P-256, P-384 or P-521 Key agreement with the protection key

Other protection keys, such as Ed25519 or ML-DSA, cannot receive the key. The call then fails before it sends anything.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The client accepts the key only when its signature verifies with the signer certificate in the key package and the key matches the public key of the issued certificate. With WithTrustedCAs the signer certificate must also chain to the trusted CAs and either assert id-kp-cmKGA, be a CA certificate or be the certificate that protected the response. Without trusted CAs the client does not validate the signer, which RFC 9483 section 4.1.6 allows for a MAC-protected exchange.

When a check fails, the client rejects the certificate in its certConf and returns an error. When the certConf itself fails after the checks, the ConfirmationError holds the key in GeneratedKey next to the certificate.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
EnrollResult.GeneratedKey holds the key:

Field Content PrivateKey The parsed key: *rsa.PrivateKey, *ecdsa.PrivateKey, ed25519.PrivateKey, *mldsa.PrivateKey or a composite ML-DSA key. It is nil for a key type the client cannot parse, such as ML-KEM PKCS8 The DER PKCS #8 key. A OneAsymmetricKey version 2 from the CA keeps its public key Signer The certificate of the key generation authority that signed the key

An ML-KEM key is checked against the certificate through the public key that its OneAsymmetricKey carries.

docs.title: Delayed delivery
docs.text: The CA may answer with status waiting. The key then arrives with the certificate when the client polls. With WithDeferredPolling, PendingEnrollment.CentralKeyGeneration is true and ResumeEnrollment needs the same credentials to decrypt the key.

docs.title: Protocol version
docs.text: These requests are sent as CMP version 3 (cmp2021), because the CA answers with EnvelopedData. The client reads the key package in both forms a CA may send: the AsymmetricKeyPackage of RFC 9810 section 5.2.2 and the id-data that OpenSSL writes, which may hold a PKCS #1 or SEC 1 key. A private key in the deprecated EncryptedValue format is refused.

docs.title: Enrollment
docs.text:
The client package requests certificates with the four CMP enrollment messages. Each call runs the whole exchange: protection, response verification, polling and certificate confirmation.

Method Message Use SendIR ir First certificate of a device, usually with a shared secret SendCR cr Another certificate for a device that already has one SendKUR kur Replace a certificate, signed with the certificate being replaced SendP10CR p10cr Send an existing PKCS #10 CSR

Keys that cannot sign, such as ML-KEM, use the methods in Keys that cannot sign. A device that lets the CA generate its key pair uses the methods in Keys the CA generates.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Every request is protected with a pkicmp.Credentials:

  • pkicmp.NewMACCredentials(secret) protects with a shared secret. It uses PBMAC1 by default. pkicmp.WithPBM() selects PasswordBasedMac and pkicmp.WithPBMAlgorithms(crypto.SHA1, crypto.SHA1) selects the SHA-1 suite that RFC 4210 peers expect.
  • pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(key, cert, chain...) signs with an existing certificate. The chain is sent in extraCerts so the CA can verify the certificate. The digest follows the key type. WithHash on the credentials chooses SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 for an RSA or ECDSA key, for example for a CA that expects one algorithm.

A MAC-protected request names its secret through the sender name or the reference in senderKID. A new device usually has no name yet, so set client.WithSenderKID to the reference the CA gave you.

docs.title: Initial enrollment
docs.text:
key, _ := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
creds, _ := pkicmp.NewMACCredentials([]byte("my-shared-secret"))

// A bootstrapping device has no trust anchor yet. Add client.WithTrustedCAs when
// one is available, so that a signed rejection can be verified.
c := client.NewClient("http://localhost:8080/cmp")
result, err := c.SendIR(context.Background(), key, creds,
    client.WithSenderKID([]byte("my-device")),
    client.WithTemplateSubject(pkix.Name{CommonName: "my-device"}),
)

result.Certificate is the issued certificate. result.CAPubs holds the CA certificates from the response. The client trusts them to verify the issued certificate only when the response was MAC-protected, as RFC 9810 section 5.3.2 allows and a device can keep them as its first trust anchors under the same condition. Response verification explains when the client needs WithTrustedCAs.

docs.title: Key update
docs.text:
creds, _ := pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(existingKey, existingCert)
c := client.NewClient("http://localhost:8080/cmp", client.WithTrustedCAs(trustedCAs))

result, err := c.SendKUR(context.Background(), newKey, creds)

With SignatureCredentials, SendKUR names existingCert in the CRMF oldCertID control. The sender and the template subject repeat its subject with the bytes the certificate encodes, so a CA that compares names byte by byte finds them unchanged. A certificate with an empty subject is renewed with a NULL-DN subject and its subjectAltName. WithOldCertificate sets the certificate for custom credential types and WithSender and WithTemplateSubject override either name.

docs.title: Request options
docs.text:
Request options apply to one call:

Option Effect WithSender Sender name in the header. A signed request otherwise names the subject of its certificate WithSenderKID senderKID in every message of the call, the reference of a shared secret WithTemplateSubject Subject in the certificate template WithTemplateExtension Adds an extension to the template, such as subjectAltName WithTemplateValidity Asks for a validity period in the template. The CA decides the validity it grants WithCertProfile Names a certificate profile in the header (RFC 9483 section 3.1) WithOldCertificate The certificate a key update replaces WithGeneralInfo Adds items to generalInfo of the header, such as a vendor profile identifier WithCertReqID The certReqId of the request, which the CA repeats in its answer. Default 0 WithPOPHash The digest of the signature proof of possession of an RSA or ECDSA key WithImplicitConfirm Asks for implicit confirmation, so that a CA that grants it needs no certConf

Many CAs route requests on the recipient name and refuse a request without one. Set client.WithRecipient on the client whenever the CA name is known. Client options lists every client and request option.

docs.title: Waiting and polling
docs.text:
A CA that cannot issue at once answers with status waiting. The method then polls with pollReq until the CA decides, sends certConf and returns. It waits the checkAfter the CA asks for, clamped by WithCheckAfterLimits to between 1 second and 1 hour by default and gives up after WithMaxPolls attempts, 60 by default.

Give every call a context with a deadline. It is the only bound on the whole operation, because the CA chooses each wait.

WithDeferredPolling collects the certificate later instead, for example from a job that runs again the next day. The method returns at the first waiting answer with EnrollResult.Pending set. PendingEnrollment encodes to JSON and holds no key or secret, but anyone with it and the credentials can collect the certificate, so store it like the credentials.

result, err := c.SendIR(ctx, key, creds, client.WithDeferredPolling())
if err == nil && result.Pending != nil {
    state, _ := json.Marshal(result.Pending)
    // Store state and run again later.
}

// Later, possibly in another process, with the same credentials and trust settings:
var pending client.PendingEnrollment
_ = json.Unmarshal(state, &pending)
result, err = c.ResumeEnrollment(ctx, &pending, creds)
if pendingErr, ok := errors.AsType[*client.PendingError](err); ok {
    // The CA still waits. Store pendingErr.Pending and try again later.
}

ResumeEnrollment waits until PendingEnrollment.NextPoll, polls until the CA decides, checks the certificate and confirms it as the Send* methods do. Under WithDeferredPolling it sends one pollReq and returns the next state while the CA still waits. A Send* method without the option returns a PendingError when polling stops at the deadline, at WithMaxPolls or when a pollReq gets no answer, and its state resumes the same way. A request that proves possession with EncryptedCertificate is resumed with ResumeEnrollmentWithIndirectPOP and its private key.

Always store the state from the latest call. The CA checks that each pollReq answers its last pollRep, so an older state is refused with badRecipientNonce. The same happens when a pollReq reached the CA but its answer was lost.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
The method confirms an issued certificate with certConf and waits for pkiConf before it returns. WithImplicitConfirm adds implicitConfirm to the request header (RFC 9810 section 5.1.1.1), which asks the CA to skip that round trip. A CA that agrees repeats the item in its certificate response. The method then returns with EnrollResult.ImplicitConfirm set and sends nothing more, because the CA has closed the transaction. A CA that wants the confirmation leaves the item out and the method confirms as usual. RFC 9483 section 4.1.1 asks an end entity to request implicit confirmation unless it needs the confirmation.

A grant the request did not ask for is honored as well, as OpenSSL does, since the CA would refuse a certConf for a closed transaction. A certificate the client refuses after a grant is not reported to the CA, as RFC 9483 section 3.6.1 asks. The option applies to ir, cr, kur and p10cr and is ignored by SendRR and the general messages.

docs.title: Results and errors
docs.text:
Error Meaning *pkicmp.PKIStatusError The CA refused the request in a verified response. pkicmp.HasFailure(err, pkicmp.FailBadPOP) tests a failure bit *client.UnverifiedStatusError The CA refused in a signed error the client could not verify, usually because no trust anchor is set. Log it, do not act on it *client.ConfirmationError The CA issued a certificate but the certConf exchange failed. The error holds the certificate and the key the CA generated for a request for central key generation *client.PendingError Polling stopped while the CA still had the request waiting. Pending resumes it with ResumeEnrollment *client.Error A transport or verification failure, with the failed step in Op

pkicmp.HasFailure never reports bits from an unverified message.

A ConfirmationError needs care. The CA may keep the certificate or revoke it as unconfirmed, so check the CA before retrying, because a retry may issue a second certificate.

The client rejects an issued certificate that does not certify the requested key, does not chain to the trust anchors or carries the wrong certReqId. It reports the rejection to the CA in certConf before it returns the error. It does not compare the subject, because a CA may change it and answer grantedWithMods.

docs.title: Keys that cannot sign
docs.text:
ML-KEM keys and RSA or elliptic curve keys kept for encryption only cannot sign a proof of possession. They prove possession by decryption instead (RFC 9810 section 5.2.8.3). SendIRWithIndirectPOP, SendCRWithIndirectPOP and SendKURWithIndirectPOP take the private key and the method:

// The CA must support the chosen method.
kemKey, _ := mlkem.GenerateKey768()
result, err := c.SendIRWithIndirectPOP(context.Background(), kemKey, client.EncryptedCertificate, creds,
    client.WithTemplateSubject(pkix.Name{CommonName: "my-device-encryption"}),
)

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Exchange client.EncryptedCertificate The CA returns the certificate encrypted for the key. The hash in the client's certConf is the proof client.ChallengeResponse The CA first sends a popdecc challenge encrypted for the key and issues the certificate after the client returns the decrypted number

The client answers the challenge and decrypts the certificate itself. Both methods need a CA that supports them. RFC 9483 section 4.1.1 lets a CA refuse both for a key that can sign, such as RSA or an elliptic curve key.

docs.title: Accepted keys
docs.text:
Key Go type ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 *mlkem.DecapsulationKey768, *mlkem.DecapsulationKey1024 or another crypto.Decapsulator RSA *rsa.PrivateKey or another crypto.Decrypter that implements RSA-OAEP Elliptic curve on P-256, P-384 or P-521 *ecdsa.PrivateKey, *ecdh.PrivateKey or another ecdh.KeyExchanger, requested with the keyAgreement proof

ML-KEM-512 is not supported because the Go standard library does not implement it.

docs.title: Protocol version
docs.text: These requests are sent as CMP version 3 (cmp2021), because the EnvelopedData the CA answers with is cmp2021 syntax (RFC 9810 section 7). Every later message of the transaction keeps that version. A CMP version 2 CA may still send an RSA certificate in the older EncryptedValue format, which the client decrypts as well.

docs.title: Acting as a registration authority
docs.text:
A registration authority (RA) approves a request of an end entity by forwarding it inside a nested message that carries the RA's own signature (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.1). WithRegistrationAuthority makes the client do that for every request it sends:

raCreds, err := pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(raKey, raCert, raChain...)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
c := client.NewClient("https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp",
    client.WithTrustedCAs(roots),
    client.WithRegistrationAuthority(raCreds),
)
// creds protect the request itself, as the end entity would.
result, err := c.SendIR(ctx, deviceKey, creds,
    client.WithSenderKID([]byte("device-42")),
    client.WithTemplateSubject(pkix.Name{CommonName: "device-42"}),
)

docs.title: What is sent
docs.text:
• Every request of an operation goes out in its own nested message: the ir, cr, kur, p10cr, rr or genm and then each pollReq, popdecr and certConf.
  • The nested message copies the transaction ID, senderNonce and recipNonce of the request inside it. Its sender is the subject of the RA certificate. extraCerts holds the RA certificate and its chain.
  • The request inside keeps the protection made with the credentials of the Send method. The CA verifies both protections.

The CA answers the request, not the nested message, so responses are verified as without the option. A CA that refuses the RA answers with an error message, which the call returns as a *pkicmp.PKIStatusError, usually with notAuthorized.

RFC 9483 requires the RA to sign, so the option takes *pkicmp.SignatureCredentials. RFC 9810 section 4.5 marks an RA certificate with the id-kp-cmcRA extended key usage. Whether a CA requires it is CA policy.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One request per nested message. Batches of several requests (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.2) are not sent.
  • Tested against the server of this module. The OpenSSL 4.1 mock server answers a nested message with "unsupported pkibody".

The server side is described in Registration authorities.

docs.title: Response verification
docs.text: The client verifies every response before it acts on it. This page explains what it checks, which trust material it needs and the options for CAs that deviate from RFC 9483.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
• A MAC-protected response is verified with the shared secret of the request credentials.
  • A signature-protected response is verified against the anchors in client.WithTrustedCAs. The signer certificate must chain to them and its subject must match the sender in the response header.

Either mechanism is accepted by default, because many CAs authenticate a device by shared secret and sign every response. client.WithResponseProtection pins one mechanism, as RFC 9483 section 3.1 asks.

docs.title: Trust anchors
docs.text:
Set WithTrustedCAs wherever an anchor is available:

c := client.NewClient("https://ca.example.com/.well-known/cmp/p/devices",
    client.WithTrustedCAs(trustedCAs),
    client.WithRecipient(pkix.Name{CommonName: "Device Issuing CA"}),
)

A shared-secret enrollment can complete without a pool, which is how a device gets its first anchor from caPubs. Errors are signed however the request was protected (RFC 9810 section 5.3.21), so without a pool a rejection such as transactionIdInUse arrives as an UnverifiedStatusError: safe to log, not to act on. A CA that signs every response cannot be used without a pool at all.

When the anchors are known out of band, WithoutCAPubsTrust keeps caPubs out of them. The issued certificate must then chain to the pool. result.CAPubs still holds the certificates.

The pool also validates the issued certificate. A CA with a composite ML-DSA or SLH-DSA key is trusted as an issuer only when the response also carries its certificate in extraCerts or caPubs. The pool entry still decides whether that certificate is trusted.

docs.title: Signer certificate
docs.text:
The signer certificate comes from extraCerts. A server may send extraCerts only on its first response, so the client keeps the certificate it authenticated earlier in the operation and tries it for later messages under the same checks.

Some CAs need extra options:

CA behavior Symptom Option Signs a response, such as the answer to a revocation request, without attaching its certificate pkicmp.ReasonNoCandidateSigner WithServerCerts with the certificate the CA signs with, often the issuing CA Copies the request's senderKID into the response pkicmp.ReasonSenderKIDMismatch WithSenderKIDMismatch Signs with SHA-1 pkicmp.ReasonUnsupportedAlgorithm WithSHA1Signatures Uses a MAC iteration count outside 100 to 1000000, or a PBMAC1 key length that multiplies it past the maximum The MAC parameters are refused WithMACIterationLimits

WithServerCerts does not trust a certificate directly. Like every candidate, it must chain to the anchors, match the sender name and verify the signature. WithSHA1Signatures covers only the message signature. Certificates signed with SHA-1 are still refused by crypto/x509.

docs.title: Certificate responses
docs.text:
A certificate response must hold exactly one CertResponse with the certReqId of the request. A p10cr has none, so both -1 and 0 are accepted. The issued certificate must certify the requested public key and validate against the anchors, with the response extraCerts completing the path.

The subject is not compared with the request, because a CA may change it and answer grantedWithMods. A certificate that fails these checks is rejected in certConf before the error is returned, so the CA learns about it at once.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
The client posts to the endpoint with Content-Type: application/pkixcmp. A CMP message in an HTTP 4xx or 5xx response is parsed and verified before its status is returned and the error keeps the HTTP status. Response bodies are limited to 10 MiB by default, set with WithMaxResponseBytes.

The default HTTP client gives up on an exchange after 120 seconds, client.DefaultHTTPTimeout, so a CA that accepts the connection and never answers does not hold the call until the context expires. WithHTTPClient supplies another HTTP client, for example with a TLS configuration or another timeout.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
Client.SendRR asks the CA to revoke a certificate (RFC 9483 section 4.2). RFC 9483 expects the request to be signed with the certificate being revoked:

creds, _ := pkicmp.NewSignatureCredentials(certKey, cert)

// Some CAs sign the response without attaching their certificate. WithServerCerts
// supplies it, and it must still chain to trustedCAs and match the response sender.
c := client.NewClient("http://localhost:8080/cmp",
    client.WithTrustedCAs(trustedCAs),
    client.WithServerCerts([]*x509.Certificate{issuingCA}),
)

err := c.SendRR(context.Background(), cert, pkicmp.CRLReasonKeyCompromise, creds)
if pkicmp.HasFailure(err, pkicmp.FailCertRevoked) {
    // The certificate was already revoked.
}

A nil error means the CA revoked the certificate. A refusal arrives as a *pkicmp.PKIStatusError.

A registration authority or another management entity that revokes for an end entity signs with its own credentials (RFC 9483 section 5.3.2). The CA decides whether it may.

docs.title: Revocation by serial number
docs.text:
A requester that has no copy of the certificate, such as an operator who knows only its serial number and the CA, names it with Client.SendRRBySerial:

serial, _ := new(big.Int).SetString("1A2B", 16)
err := c.SendRRBySerial(context.Background(), pkix.Name{CommonName: "Example CA"}, serial,
    pkicmp.CRLReasonKeyCompromise, raCreds)

The issuer name is encoded from the pkix.Name. A CA that compares the name bytes needs the attributes in the order and with the string types of the certificate. The server package compares the decoded attributes, so the string types may differ there.

docs.title: Invalidity date
docs.text:
WithInvalidityDate adds the invalidityDate CRL entry extension (RFC 5280 section 5.3.2) to the request: the time at which the key is known or suspected to have been compromised or the certificate otherwise became invalid. A CA may publish it in the CRL entry. It is sent as a GeneralizedTime in UTC with a resolution of one second.

err := c.SendRR(context.Background(), cert, pkicmp.CRLReasonKeyCompromise, creds,
    client.WithInvalidityDate(time.Date(2026, 10, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)))

docs.title: Holds
docs.text: pkicmp.CRLReasonCertificateHold suspends a certificate and pkicmp.CRLReasonRemoveFromCRL releases it, if the CA supports holds.

docs.title: Delayed answers
docs.text: A CA that waits for a decision, for example an operator's approval, answers with status waiting. The client polls as it does for enrollment and returns once the CA decides. A revocation has no certConf.

docs.title: Signer certificate in the response
docs.text: Some CAs, including some Nokia NCM releases, sign the revocation response with the issuing CA key without attaching that certificate. Pass the issuer of the revoked certificate to WithServerCerts. Response verification explains the checks it still has to pass.

docs.title: Support messages
docs.text:
General messages ask the CA for information rather than a certificate (RFC 9483 section 4.3):

Method Returns GetCACertificates Intermediate and issuing CA certificates GetRootCAUpdate A new root certificate, certified by the current one GetCertReqTemplate The template a request should follow, for the profile named with WithCertProfile GetCRLUpdate A CRL newer than the one the caller holds GetCurrentCRL The current CRL SendGenM The raw items of any other info type 
update, err := c.GetRootCAUpdate(context.Background(), currentRoot, creds)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, client.ErrInfoTypeNotSupported):
    // The CA does not offer root updates. RFC 4210 CAs often ignore the request.
case err != nil:
    return err
case update != nil:
    // update.NewWithNew is the new root. The client has checked that currentRoot
    // signed update.NewWithOld.
}

The other methods follow the same pattern.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• A nil result with a nil error means the CA has nothing to send, such as no newer root or CRL and no template requirements.
  • client.ErrInfoTypeNotSupported covers both a CA that lists the type as unsupported and one that leaves it out of its answer. Nokia NCM leaves every type out.
  • A CA that refuses general messages altogether answers with an error message, returned as *pkicmp.PKIStatusError. EJBCA Community Edition does this with badRequest.

docs.title: What to verify yourself
docs.text:
The response is verified like any other, so its content is as trustworthy as its protection:

  • Validate CA certificates against a trust anchor before you use them to build chains.
  • Verify a CRL signature against its issuer before you use it. GetCRLUpdate only refuses a CRL that is not newer than the one you hold, which would roll you back.
  • A root update is returned only if the current root signed the new one.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: How to build, check and change the library. Contribution rules are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go at the version go.mod declares. Every Make target runs with exactly that toolchain, which Go downloads on first use when the installed version differs.
  • Python 3 with the pinned MkDocs dependencies for the documentation site, installed by make docs-deps.
  • Docker, OpenSSL 3.2 or newer, Git and uv for the integration tests. See Testing.

Linters and other tools are downloaded into bin/ at pinned versions by the Make targets that need them.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Content pkicmp/ CMP and CRMF types, protection and verification client/ The CMP client server/ The CMP server cms/ EnvelopedData and EncryptedValue for proof of possession by decryption internal/ Path verification for composite ML-DSA chains and certificates for ML-KEM keys for the tests and the example CA, not part of the public API examples/ The mock CA and client used in Getting started test/integration/ Tests against EJBCA, OpenSSL, Nokia NCM, the Siemens CMP test suite and the Insta Certifier clients docs/ This site. docs/specs/ holds the RFC texts the code cites and is not published

docs.title: Common commands
docs.text:
make test               # go vet and the unit tests under the race detector
make lint               # golangci-lint, including the integration tests
make fuzz               # every fuzz target in pkicmp for FUZZTIME each, 30s by default
make test-integration   # every integration test, see Testing
make docs-build         # strict MkDocs build
make help               # every target

make test runs under the race detector because the documented server deployment sweeps expired transactions from a background goroutine while it serves requests. The unit tests have no external dependencies.

Run make actionlint when a workflow changes, make govulncheck when a dependency changes and make gitleaks before pushing. make tidy-check fails when go.mod or go.sum is not tidy and make fmt-check when a tracked Go file is not formatted.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from docs/ and mkdocs.yml. Set PYTHON when the MkDocs toolchain lives in a virtual environment:

make docs-deps PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
make docs-serve PYTHON=.venv/bin/python

make docs-build runs with --strict, so a broken link, a missing anchor or a page absent from the navigation fails the build. CI runs the same build on every change to the documentation and publishes the site from the default branch.

The toolchain is pinned with hashes in docs/requirements.txt, which make docs-deps installs in hash-checking mode. The direct dependencies live in docs/requirements.in. To change a version, edit that file and run make docs-requirements, which needs pip-tools in the PYTHON environment.

Package documentation on pkg.go.dev comes from the Go doc comments and make docs serves it locally with pkgsite. User-facing behavior changes belong in both places: the doc comment for the API and the relevant page here for the walkthrough. Getting started includes the example programs from examples/, so change the program and the page follows.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
.editorconfig records the whitespace rules: UTF-8, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace, tabs for Go and Make recipes, four spaces for shell, Python and Robot Framework files and two spaces for YAML and TOML. LICENSE, the RFC texts under docs/specs/ and the EJBCA profile exports stay verbatim.

Protocol changes need negative tests and an RFC citation. A change must keep working against real CMP peers and against clients that implement only RFC 4210. Interoperability claims need sanitized evidence naming the peer and its version.

docs.title: Release process
docs.text: A release is started by pushing a version tag that is reachable from main and by nothing else. RELEASE_NOTES.md carries one section per version and that section becomes the release description.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: The module follows semantic versioning under the Compatibility policy. Release headings use ## vX.Y.Z - D Mon YYYY, for example ## v0.4.0 - 11 Oct 2026, with an unpadded day and an abbreviated English month. Keep TBD until the release date is set.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Set the release date in RELEASE_NOTES.md and merge dev into main.

  2. Run the release check on main:

    make release-check VERSION=vX.Y.Z

    It exports HEAD with git archive into a new temporary directory, builds, vets and tests the export and imports it from a separate module, so it catches files that are ignored, untracked or only present locally. It also checks the release notes heading. Set RELEASE_CHECK_DIR to a path that does not exist yet to keep the export somewhere else.

  3. Tag the release commit on main and push the tag:

    git push origin vX.Y.Z

  4. The release workflow repeats the check on the tag and creates a draft release with the release notes section as its description. Review the draft and publish it.

Never draft a release in the GitHub UI

Drafting there creates the tag, which starts the workflow against a release that is already published. The workflow refuses to rebuild a published release, so the release and its tag have to be removed before the tag can be pushed again.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The documentation workflow publishes this site from the default branch to GitHub Pages whenever docs/, mkdocs.yml or the examples change there. Pull requests and pushes to dev run the strict build without publishing. The site therefore describes main, which is the latest release plus any fixes merged since.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The library is tested at three levels: unit tests in each package, fuzz targets over the message parser and protection checks and integration tests against independent CMP implementations.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
make test

Runs go vet and every unit test under the race detector. The server tests drive complete flows through the handler, including delayed issuance, confirmation, revocation, nested messages, snapshots and the compatibility options. The client tests run against an in-process server. The unit tests have no external dependencies.

docs.title: Fuzzing
docs.text:
make fuzz
make fuzz FUZZTIME=10m

Fuzzes whole-message parsing, MAC protection parameters and signature verification in pkicmp, each for FUZZTIME. Separate targets cover SLH-DSA keys, PKCS #10 requests, proofs of possession, certificate signatures, message protection and root CA key updates. CI runs 30 seconds per target. Go writes a failing input under pkicmp/testdata/fuzz. Commit that input with the fix so it stays a regression test.

Minimization is off by default, because a worker still minimizing when FUZZTIME expires makes Go report the run as failed. Set FUZZMINIMIZETIME to a duration such as 1m to minimize a crashing input.

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
The integration tests need Docker, OpenSSL 3.2 or newer, Git and uv:

make setup             # start the EJBCA container and clone the CMP test suite
make test-integration  # run every integration test
make teardown          # stop and remove the EJBCA container
Target Peer Needs make test-integration-ejbca EJBCA as the CA for the client make setup-ejbca make test-integration-openssl OpenSSL cmp and cms in both directions OpenSSL 3.2 or newer on the path make test-integration-cmp-test-suite The Siemens CMP test suite against the server make setup-cmp-test-suite make test-integration-ncm A Nokia NCM instance The NCM_CMP_* variables make test-integration-certifier The Insta Certifier 10 cmpclient and the Insta Certifier 7 ssh-cmpclient against the server A local client image

Some OpenSSL cases need a newer release and skip on older ones:

  • The certificate request template test against the OpenSSL mock server needs OpenSSL 4.0, because the OpenSSL 3 server crashes on that request.
  • The ML-KEM cases of the CMS and proof of possession tests need OpenSSL 4.0, the first release with ML-KEM in CMS.
  • The elliptic curve case of the encrypted certificate test needs OpenSSL 3.5, because earlier releases cannot read a certificate in EnvelopedData.

CI runs the OpenSSL tests with 3.5 and 4.0. Its OpenSSL builds have no openssl.cnf, so make test-integration-openssl points OPENSSL_CONF to a missing file. A test that needs the local openssl.cnf then fails locally too. Plain go test still reads your openssl.cnf.

The Insta Certifier 10 cmpclient and the Insta Certifier 7 ssh-cmpclient are proprietary, so CI does not run them. The tests need a local image built from your own copies. Both clients break RFC 4211 and RFC 9483 rules in places. The tests check that the server defaults refuse those requests and that the matching option accepts them:

docs.title: Collecting diagnostics
docs.text:
Before asking for help, collect:

  • the go-pki-cmp and Go versions
  • the CMP peer and its version
  • the request type and the message protection
  • the error the library returned and the PKIStatusInfo the peer sent
  • the peer's log lines around the failure

Never share shared secrets, private keys, full CSRs, CMP messages captured from a production system or production endpoint details. SUPPORT.md says where to post.

docs.title: Messages and protection
docs.text: The pkicmp package is the base of the module. It defines the CMP and CRMF types, builds and parses messages and applies and verifies their protection. The client and server packages build on it. Use it directly for custom tooling, a registration authority proxy or tests.

docs.title: Building a message
docs.text:
PKIMessage corresponds to the ASN.1 PKIMessage. Create one from a body and header options:

body := pkicmp.NewPKIConfBody()
msg := pkicmp.NewPKIMessage(body, pkicmp.MessageOptions{
    Sender:     sender,
    Recipient:  recipient,
    RecipNonce: previous.Header.SenderNonce,
})

The transaction ID and senderNonce default to 128 random bits (RFC 9810 section 5.1.1) and messageTime to the current time. Body constructors such as NewIRBody, NewIPBody and NewGenMBody wrap each CHOICE variant. PKIBody keeps the raw DER and decodes it only when a typed getter such as PKIBody.IR is called.

PKIMessage.MarshalBinary and pkicmp.ParsePKIMessage are the only points where messages become bytes and back.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Credentials applies protection:

creds, err := pkicmp.NewMACCredentials([]byte("shared-secret"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := creds.Protect(msg); err != nil {
    return err
}
Credentials Protection NewMACCredentials PBMAC1 by default, the algorithm RFC 9481 section 7 recommends. WithPBM selects PasswordBasedMac and WithPBMAlgorithms its hash functions NewSignatureCredentials A signature with an X.509 certificate and key. The chain is sent in extraCerts. The digest follows the key type unless WithHash chooses one

To answer a MAC-protected message with the same algorithm suite, as RFC 9483 section 3.2 requires, pass VerifyResult.ProtectionParams from the verified request to NewMACCredentials. It reuses the suite with a fresh salt.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
PKIMessage.Verify checks the protection:

result, err := msg.Verify(pkicmp.VerifyOptions{
    SharedSecret:       []byte("shared-secret"),
    TrustPool:          trustedCAs,
    RequiredProtection: pkicmp.ProtectionSignature,
})

With both a secret and a trust pool, the message decides which is used. Set RequiredProtection to pin one mechanism, as RFC 9483 section 3.1 asks within one operation. The zero value accepts either.

A signature check also binds the protection certificate to the sender: when the header sender is a directory name, it must equal the certificate subject (RFC 9483 section 3.5). A NULL-DN sender is accepted on the trust chain alone.

Option Effect ExtraCerts, TrustedCert Candidate signer certificates beyond those the message carries SenderKID, AllowSenderKIDMismatch Select candidates by subject key identifier or try all of them CurrentTime Validate the certificates at another time, such as when a recorded message arrived AllowSHA1Signatures Accept SHA-1 signatures, refused by default MinMACIterationCount, MaxMACIterationCount Bound the MAC iteration count, 100 to 1000000 by default. For PBMAC1 the maximum covers the iterations multiplied by the PRF blocks of the key length RequireDigitalSignatureKeyUsage Require the digitalSignature bit that RFC 9483 section 3.5 asks for. Deployed CAs often lack it

Do not take CurrentTime from the message when the result decides whether to act on it, because the sender sets its messageTime.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error is typed and carries an InvalidReason:

Type Meaning ParseError Malformed message, missing field or a parameter outside the accepted range. When the failure comes after a readable header, its Header field holds that header, so a server can answer with an error message ProtectionError Protection could not be applied VerificationError Bad MAC or signature, wrong mechanism, sender mismatch or no certificate to verify with

Common verification reasons:

Reason Cause ReasonBadMAC The MAC does not match the shared secret ReasonUnexpectedProtection The message used another mechanism than RequiredProtection ReasonSenderMismatch No candidate certificate has the sender's name ReasonUntrustedSigner No candidate with the sender's name chains to the trust pool ReasonNoCandidateSigner No certificate was available to verify the signature ReasonSenderKIDMismatch The senderKID names none of the candidate certificates ReasonUnsupportedAlgorithm The algorithm is unknown or disabled, such as SHA-1

PKIStatusInfo.AsError turns a peer status into a *pkicmp.PKIStatusError, and pkicmp.HasFailure(err, bit) tests its failure bits.

docs.title: Your responsibilities
docs.text:
The package verifies protection and parses CMP. It does not implement a client or CA policy. When you use it directly:

  • Pin the mechanism you expect on the message you verify, which is not always the one you send with. Holding both kinds of trust material under the default lets a peer pick the weaker one.
  • Keep the protection certificate across a transaction. extraCerts may appear only on the first response, so pass VerifyResult.ProtectionCertificate back through ExtraCerts or TrustedCert.
  • Bind the issued certificate to the request by comparing its public key with the key you asked for. Subjects may differ under grantedWithMods.
  • Trust caPubs only when VerifyResult.MACVerified is set (RFC 9810 section 5.3.2).
  • Clamp checkAfter yourself. PollRepContent holds the peer's value as sent.
  • Sanitize peer text before logging. PKIStatusInfo.AsError joins the free text without validating UTF-8 or removing control characters.

docs.title: Certificate confirmation
docs.text: pkicmp.NewCertStatus computes the certificate hash for a manual certConf, including the explicit hash identifier that ML-DSA and composite ML-DSA certificates need.

docs.text: Options of client.NewClient apply to every call of that client. Request options apply to one call. The package documentation describes each in full.

docs.text:
Option Default Effect WithTrustedCAs None Anchors for signed responses and issued certificates WithRecipient NULL-DN CA name in the request header. Many CAs route on it WithResponseProtection pkicmp.ProtectionAny Requires MAC or signature protection on every response WithExtraCerts None Certificates added to extraCerts of every request WithServerCerts None CA protection certificates known out of band, for responses that do not carry them WithoutCAPubsTrust Off Keeps the CA certificates in caPubs of a MAC-protected response from becoming anchors WithSenderKIDMismatch Off Accepts a signed response whose senderKID names none of the candidate certificates WithSHA1Signatures Off Accepts responses signed with SHA-1 WithMACIterationLimits 100 to 1000000 Accepted MAC iteration counts in responses, for PBMAC1 multiplied by the PRF blocks of the key length WithMaxPolls 60 Poll attempts before the call gives up WithCheckAfterLimits 1 second to 1 hour Clamps each wait the CA asks for WithMaxResponseBytes 10 MiB Largest accepted response body. Zero or less disables the limit WithHTTPClient The default transport with a 120 second timeout The HTTP client, for TLS settings, a proxy or another timeout WithRegistrationAuthority Off Wraps every request in a nested message signed by a registration authority

To send a MAC iteration count outside the default range, set it on the credentials with pkicmp.WithMACIterationCount and widen pkicmp.WithMACIterationLimits to match.

docs.text:
Option Effect WithSender Sender name in the header. A signed request otherwise names the subject of its protection certificate WithSenderKID senderKID in every message, the reference of a shared secret WithTemplateSubject Subject in the certificate template WithTemplateExtension Adds an extension to the certificate template WithTemplateValidity Asks for a notBefore, a notAfter or both in the certificate template of an ir, cr or kur. The CA decides the validity it grants WithCertProfile Names a certificate profile in the header WithOldCertificate The certificate a key update replaces, for custom credential types WithGeneralInfo Adds items to generalInfo of the request header, after the certProfile WithCertReqID The certReqId of an ir, cr or kur, which the CA must repeat. Default 0 WithPOPHash The digest of the signature proof of possession of an RSA or ECDSA key. Default by key type WithDeferredPolling Returns an ir, cr, kur or p10cr at the first waiting answer with the state for ResumeEnrollment WithImplicitConfirm Asks for implicit confirmation. When the CA grants it, no certConf is sent and EnrollResult.ImplicitConfirm is true WithInvalidityDate Adds the invalidityDate CRL entry extension to a revocation request, the time the certificate became invalid

docs.title: Test aids
docs.text:
These request options send deliberately wrong messages, to test how a CA handles them. They change nothing unless given. Do not use them in production.

Option Effect WithCertConfStatus Sends a statusInfo in the certConf, such as a rejection. A CA must answer a rejection with pkiConf (RFC 9483 section 3.6.1). The call then returns the certificate WithMessageMutator Changes every message of the call before it is protected: the first request and any popdecr, pollReq and certConf. The function gets the message and the response it answers WithProtectedMessageMutator Changes every message after it is protected and before the nested message of WithRegistrationAuthority wraps it, for example to remove the protection

The client verifies each response against the message as changed. A mutator that returns an error stops the call before the message is sent. A changed certConf that the CA refuses ends in a ConfirmationError that holds the certificate. ResumeEnrollment applies them to its pollReq and certConf messages. Its first pollReq answers a response the client did not keep, so the mutators get nil for it.

// Send a certConf whose certHash does not match the certificate.
wrongHash := client.WithMessageMutator(func(msg, _ *pkicmp.PKIMessage) error {
    if msg.Body.Type != pkicmp.BodyTypeCertConf {
        return nil
    }
    conf, err := msg.Body.CertConf()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    (*conf)[0].CertHash[0] ^= 0xff
    msg.Body = pkicmp.NewCertConfBody(conf)
    return nil
})
_, err := c.SendIR(ctx, key, creds, wrongHash)
// A CA that follows RFC 9483 refuses it with badCertId.

docs.title: Compatibility policy
docs.text: The module uses semantic versioning. The public API is every exported identifier of pkicmp, client, server and cms. The internal packages, the examples and the integration tests are not part of it.

docs.title: Before v1.0.0
docs.text: A minor release may change the public API. The release notes name every such change and what callers need to do. Patch releases keep the API.

docs.title: Rules for every release
docs.text:
• Structs may gain fields. Construct them with field names.
  • Enumerations may gain values. Request types, statuses, failure bits, verification reasons and proof of possession methods may grow. Switch statements over them need a default case.
  • Refusal reasons may become more precise. A failure that used to report one InvalidReason may report a new, narrower one. Check for the reasons you act on and treat the rest as a failure.
  • New server capabilities use optional interfaces or options. The server detects an interface your CA implements, so existing CAs keep compiling.
  • Wire behavior changes are announced. Behavior a peer can observe changes only with a release notes entry and an RFC citation.

docs.text:
1. Read the release notes section for the new version.

  3. Run your own integration tests against the CMP peers you support. Tested implementations names the peers each feature was tested with.
