docs.title: Security model
docs.text: What the library checks, what it assumes about your application and where you must add your own controls.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Untrusted
    Client[CMP client]
    RA[Registration authority]
  end
  subgraph Library
    Server[server.Server]
  end
  subgraph Application
    Lookups[(Secret and certificate store)]
    Policy[Policy middleware]
    CA[CA]
  end
  Client -->|protected messages| Server
  RA -->|nested messages| Server
  Server --> Lookups
  Server --> Policy
  Server --> CA

Clients and registration authorities are untrusted until their protection is verified. The lookups, the policy and the CA are trusted application code.

On the client side the CA is untrusted until its response is verified against your anchors or the shared secret.

docs.title: What the server enforces
docs.text:
Message authentication. Every message is verified before your code sees it: a MAC with the secret your lookup returns or a signature with the certificate it returns. A signed message must name the certificate subject as its sender. The MAC key derivation work is bounded before it runs and an RSA key above 16384 bits is refused before any public key operation, so an unauthenticated request cannot buy unbounded work.

Transaction binding. Transactions are keyed by the verified credential and the transaction ID. For a MAC-protected client the credential is the shared secret itself, so a sender name cannot buy a second quota. Every message after the first must repeat the previous senderNonce. One client cannot continue, confirm or poll another client's transaction.

Proof of possession. A certificate is never issued for a key the requester did not prove holding, with or without a policy. An encrypted certificate counts as delivered only after a certConf with its hash.

Revocation authority. By default only the certificate being revoked may sign its revocation. Everything else goes to your RevocationAuthorizer.

Error disclosure. An error your code returns that is not a *server.Error becomes a bare systemFailure. Its text never reaches the peer.

Bounded parsing. Request bodies, transaction counts and snapshot sizes are limited. Every parser in pkicmp reads bytes a peer chose, before anything establishes who that peer is, so the whole-message parser, MAC parameters, signature verification and the SLH-DSA key and signature checks have fuzz targets that CI runs.

docs.title: What the client enforces
docs.text:
• Every response is verified with the shared secret or against the trust anchors.
  • The transaction ID, nonces and certReqId must match the request.
  • The issued certificate must certify the requested key and chain to the anchors.
  • A centrally generated private key must carry a valid signature and match the issued certificate. With trust anchors its signer must chain to them and be a key generation authority.
  • caPubs extend the anchors only for a MAC-protected response and never with WithoutCAPubsTrust.
  • Waits between polls are clamped and the response size is limited.
  • An unverified error status is reported as UnverifiedStatusError and never as a PKIStatusError, so code that acts on failure bits cannot be steered by a forged error.

docs.title: What your application must provide
docs.text: Concern Your responsibility Authorization Middleware or IssueCertificate decides who may request which certificate. Without it any authenticated client gets any name Unique shared secret references Two clients with one reference cannot be told apart Certificate store CertificateLookup returns only certificates you trust and no revoked ones Certificate contents Remove requested extensions before you set your own and check every subject attribute CA key protection WithSigner takes a crypto.Signer, so the key can stay in an HSM Encrypted certificates Publish only after ConfirmAccepted and revoke on ConfirmExpired or ConfirmRejected Central key generation The KeyGenerator keeps no copy of a private key it hands out unless your key archive policy needs one. The key generation authority key is protected like the CA key Registration authorities The RAAuthorizer must identify the RA itself, not only a valid protection Transport TLS if the deployment needs confidentiality. CMP protection gives integrity and authentication only Rate limiting and audit Middleware. The library has no rate limits beyond the transaction caps Durable state Snapshots and a response cache when the server must survive restarts or retries

docs.title: Options that weaken checks
docs.text:
The compatibility options in Policy and client compatibility each relax one rule. They keep the checks that authenticate a request, but some remove a binding:

  • WithPoposkInputVariants accepts a proof that does not cover the template, so only the message protection binds the requested names to the key holder.
  • WithOptionalPollReqRecipNonce lets a recorded pollReq of the same transaction collect the final response. That response holds no secret in the clear. A centrally generated key in it is encrypted for the requester.
  • WithMACRevocation lets a shared secret revoke. Your RevocationAuthorizer decides which certificates.
  • WithSHA1Signatures accepts a deprecated hash.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Report suspected vulnerabilities privately as SECURITY.md describes. Only the latest release receives fixes.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The server verifies the protection of every message before your code sees it. It has no credential store of its own. You supply two lookups:

  • WithSecretLookup finds the shared secret of a MAC-protected message.
  • WithCertificateLookup finds the certificate of a signature-protected message.

Without a lookup, messages with that kind of protection are refused: MAC-protected ones with badMessageCheck and signed ones with signerNotTrusted.

docs.title: Shared secrets
docs.text:
type SecretLookup interface {
    LookupSecret(sender pkix.Name, senderKID []byte) ([]byte, error)
}

RFC 9810 section 5.1.1 covers two cases:

  • Known sender. The sender field carries the name and senderKID should be set. Either or both may locate the secret.
  • Unknown sender, usually a first enrollment. The sender is a NULL-DN and senderKID carries the reference number of the secret (RFC 4210 section 5.1.3.1).

The reference and the secret work like a user name and a password. Two clients that share a reference cannot be told apart and one could obtain certificates in the other's name. Enforce unique references when you provision secrets:

func Register(senderKID, secret []byte) error {
    if exists(senderKID) {
        return errors.New("senderKID already registered")
    }
    store[string(senderKID)] = secret
    return nil
}

The server keeps a MAC client's transactions and its share of WithMaxTransactionsPerCredential apart from other clients by the shared secret itself, whichever field the lookup used to find it. The sender name and senderKID a request carries do not select the quota, so one secret cannot get a second quota by naming a different sender. Clients that share one secret share one quota. Clients that send only a name, as RFC 4210 allows, keep separate transactions as long as their secrets differ.

The client chooses the MAC iteration count and the server runs every iteration before it can check the MAC. WithMACIterationLimits bounds that work, 100 to 1000000 by default. For PBMAC1 the maximum bounds the whole PBKDF2 derivation, the iterations multiplied by the number of PRF output blocks the requested key length needs, so a long key from a short PRF cannot multiply the work. A request outside the range is refused with badMessageCheck and the text "MAC protection parameters not accepted" before any key derivation. The minimum is the 100 that RFC 4211 section 4.4 requires. Lower it only for a peer that sends fewer: a small count makes an offline guess of a weak secret cheap.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
type CertificateLookup interface {
    LookupCertificate(issuer pkix.Name, subject pkix.Name, senderKID []byte) (*x509.Certificate, error)
}

issuer is the recipient in the header, subject the sender and senderKID the key identifier. Any of them may be empty. The names are lookup keys only: the server verifies the signature against the certificate you return, so a client that lies about its name either finds nothing or fails the signature check. Trust comes from your store and proof of the private key.

A senderKID that is present must name the key that signed the message (RFC 9483 section 3.5). The server compares it with the subject key identifier of the certificate you return and refuses a mismatch with badMessageCheck. This holds also when your lookup ignores senderKID, for example because it takes the signer from extraCerts. A certificate without a subject key identifier is not compared.

Return only certificates you issued or otherwise trust and do not return revoked ones.

docs.title: The sender identity
docs.text:
A verified message reaches your code with a SenderIdentity:

Field Content Certificate The signer certificate of a signature-protected message Sender The sender name. For a signed message it equals the certificate subject, so you can authorize on it SenderKID The reference of a MAC-protected message MACVerified True for a MAC-protected message RA The registration authority that forwarded the request, see Registration authorities

For a MAC-protected message the sender name is whatever resolved the secret. Authorize on SenderKID or on the name the secret is registered to.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: A request protected with an algorithm the server does not implement is refused with badAlg. This includes SHA-1 signatures, which RFC 9481 section 7.1 deprecates. WithSHA1Signatures accepts them from RFC 4210 era devices, in the protection and in the proof of possession.

docs.title: Response protection
docs.text:
The server answers a MAC-protected request with a MAC from the same secret and algorithm suite, with a fresh salt, as RFC 9483 section 3.2 requires. It repeats the client's senderKID. Responses to signed requests and to messages whose protection failed are signed with the WithSigner key.

Signing every refused request costs one signature per unauthenticated message, which matters with a slow signer such as SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s. WithUnprotectedErrorsBeforeAuthentication leaves errors raised before authentication unprotected, as RFC 9483 section 3.6.4 allows when the recipient has no credential to verify them with. A request forwarded by an authenticated registration authority is still answered with a protected error. The client of this module reports an unprotected error as UnverifiedStatusError. OpenSSL reports a missing protection instead of the status unless it runs with -unprotected_errors.

docs.title: Implementing a CA
docs.text:
The server package handles the protocol. Your code signs certificates by implementing server.CA:

type CA interface {
    IssueCertificate(ctx context.Context, reqType RequestType,
        template *x509.Certificate, sender *SenderIdentity) (*Response, error)
}

The server calls IssueCertificate for every ir, cr, kur and p10cr that passed protection, transaction, policy and proof of possession checks. reqType names the request and sender the authenticated requester.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
The template arrives with the subject, public key, extensions and subject key identifier from the request. SerialNumber is nil. The CA must set the serial number and validity and may enforce policy, change the subject, add or remove extensions or refuse the request. A validity the CRMF template asks for is not passed on.

func (c *myCA) IssueCertificate(ctx context.Context, reqType server.RequestType,
    tmpl *x509.Certificate, sender *server.SenderIdentity) (*server.Response, error) {

    serial, err := server.GenerateSerial()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    tmpl.SerialNumber = serial
    tmpl.NotBefore = time.Now()
    tmpl.NotAfter = time.Now().Add(365 * 24 * time.Hour)

    // Drop a requested keyUsage, otherwise it would override the one set below.
    oidKeyUsage := asn1.ObjectIdentifier{2, 5, 29, 15}
    tmpl.ExtraExtensions = slices.DeleteFunc(tmpl.ExtraExtensions,
        func(e pkix.Extension) bool { return e.Id.Equal(oidKeyUsage) })
    tmpl.KeyUsage = x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature

    der, err := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, tmpl, c.cert, tmpl.PublicKey, c.key)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    cert, err := x509.ParseCertificate(der)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &server.Response{Certificate: cert}, nil
}

Requested extensions win over typed fields

template.ExtraExtensions holds the extensions the requester asked for and nothing has vetted them. x509.CreateCertificate gives an extension in ExtraExtensions precedence over the matching typed field, so assigning template.KeyUsage does not override a requested keyUsage. The same applies to ExtKeyUsage, BasicConstraints and the other typed fields. Remove an extension from ExtraExtensions before you decide it yourself, as the example does.

docs.title: Subject names
docs.text:
The subject is rebuilt from pkix.Name, which drops attribute types it does not model, such as domainComponent and emailAddress. It may also reorder the rest and change their string types. server.WithRawSubject also sets template.RawSubject to the requested name, which x509.CreateCertificate issues unchanged. Clear RawSubject before you change the subject.

A request that names the entity only in a subjectAltName has an empty subject. The template marks that subjectAltName critical, as RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.6 requires. A CA that supplies a subject should clear the flag.

docs.title: Post-quantum keys
docs.text:
• A composite ML-DSA subject key arrives as *compositemldsa.PublicKey. Only compositex509.CreateCertificate from go-composite-mldsa can certify it. A CA with a composite key signs with the same function.
  • Clients can check a composite CA signature only when the CA certificate travels in the response, so pass it to WithExtraCerts or return it in Response.CACerts.
  • An ML-KEM key arrives as *mlkem.EncapsulationKey768 or *mlkem.EncapsulationKey1024, which crypto/x509 cannot certify. pkicmp.MarshalPublicKey encodes its SubjectPublicKeyInfo, whose only allowed key usage is keyEncipherment. See Keys that cannot sign.
  • An SLH-DSA key arrives as an slhdsa.PublicKey value from circl, which crypto/x509 cannot certify either. pkicmp.MarshalPublicKey encodes its SubjectPublicKeyInfo (RFC 9909). Its key usage may include digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign and cRLSign but no encipherment.
  • A CA with an SLH-DSA key signs its certificates outside crypto/x509 too, with the RFC 9909 identifier and absent parameters. It can also be the WithSigner key. Clients and the server verify paths through it and confirm its certificates with an explicit SHA-512 hash. Each signature is slow, see Known limitations.

The example CA uses compositex509.CreateCertificate, so it certifies composite keys as well as the key types crypto/x509 supports. It certifies ML-KEM keys with keyEncipherment as their only key usage.

docs.title: The response
Serving it
docs.text:
srv := server.NewCAServer(ca,
    server.LightweightPolicy(),
    server.WithSigner(caKey, caCert),
    server.WithExtraCerts([]*x509.Certificate{caCert}),
    server.WithSecretLookup(server.SecretLookupFunc(lookupSecret)),
    server.WithCertificateLookup(server.CertificateLookupFunc(lookupCertificate)),
    // A messageTime outside this tolerance is refused as badTime.
    server.WithMessageTimeTolerance(5*time.Minute),
)
if err := srv.Err(); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
http.Handle("/cmp", srv)

WithSigner takes a crypto.Signer, so the key can live in an HSM. Err reports a misconfiguration such as a signer key that does not match its certificate. Such a server answers every request with systemFailure rather than issue certificates it cannot protect, so check it at startup.

The second argument is the policy middleware. Policy and client compatibility explains LightweightPolicy and how to add your own authorization.

docs.title: Several CAs
docs.text:
Each Server serves one CA. Create one per CA and route by path. RFC 9483 section 6.1 defines the well-known path /.well-known/cmp/p/<name>:

mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.Handle("/.well-known/cmp/p/devices", devicesServer)
mux.Handle("/.well-known/cmp/p/servers", serversServer)

docs.title: Optional interfaces
docs.text:
A CA can implement more interfaces. NewCAServer detects them:

Interface Page CertificateConfirmer, PendingChecker, WaitingExpirer Delayed issuance and confirmation Revoker, RevocationAuthorizer Revocation CACertificatesProvider, RootCAUpdateProvider, CertReqTemplateProvider, CRLProvider Support messages

docs.title: Full control
docs.text: server.New takes any server.Handler, which receives the raw *pkicmp.PKIMessage and the authenticated SenderIdentity. Use it for custom routing or a proxy. Most applications should use NewCAServer, because the handler it builds also runs the proof of possession and BasicConstraints checks.

docs.title: Keys the server generates
docs.text:
WithCentralKeyGeneration lets a client ask the server to generate its key pair (RFC 9483 section 4.1.6). The certificate template of such an ir, cr or kur has no public key or an algorithm with an empty key. The request has no proof of possession. Without the option the server refuses it with badCertTemplate.

srv := server.NewCAServer(myCA, server.LightweightPolicy(),
    server.WithSigner(caKey, caCert),
    server.WithSecretLookup(myCA),
    server.WithCertificateLookup(myCA),
    server.WithCentralKeyGeneration(myGenerator, kgaKey, kgaCert),
)
if err := srv.Err(); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

docs.title: Key generator
docs.text:
server.KeyGenerator makes the key pair. GenerateKey gets the requested algorithm with its parameters and the authenticated sender. The algorithm is nil when the client leaves the choice to you. It returns the private key as DER PKCS #8 together with the public key. Return a *server.Error with badAlg for an algorithm you do not generate. A key of another algorithm than the one requested is refused with badAlg.

The server sends the key as a OneAsymmetricKey version 2 with its public key, as RFC 9483 section 4.1.6 requires.

docs.title: Key generation authority
docs.text: kgaKey signs every generated key and kgaCert is its certificate. The certificate must assert the id-kp-cmKGA extended key usage (RFC 9480 section 2.2) or be a CA certificate. OpenSSL clients accept only id-kp-cmKGA. Pass the certificates between kgaCert and the client's trust anchor as the chain, so that clients can validate the signer. Server.Err reports a key that does not match kgaCert or a certificate that may not sign keys.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
The signed key is encrypted for the requester:

Request protection Encryption MAC To the shared secret with PBKDF2 and the RFC 3211 key wrap, the only form OpenSSL reads. WithCentralKeyGenerationAESKeyWrap selects the AES key wrap of RFC 9481 section 4.3 Signature, RSA protection key Key transport with RSA-OAEP Signature, ECDSA protection key on P-256, P-384 or P-521 Key agreement with ephemeral-static ECDH Signature, other protection key Refused with badAlg

The key usage of the protection certificate is not checked.

docs.title: Signed content
docs.text: By default the server signs the OneAsymmetricKey itself as id-data. This is the form OpenSSL writes and the only one OpenSSL clients read. WithCentralKeyGenerationAsymmetricKeyPackage signs an AsymmetricKeyPackage with the id-ct-KP-aKeyPackage content type instead, as RFC 9810 section 5.2.2 and RFC 9483 section 4.1.6 specify. OpenSSL 3.5 to 4.1 clients cannot read that form.

docs.title: Your CA
docs.text:
server.POPMethodFromContext returns POPCentralKeyGeneration for these requests. The built-in CA handler of NewCAServer puts the generated public key into the template it passes to IssueCertificate. A custom Handler gets the key from server.GeneratedPublicKeyFromContext and must certify it.

The server withholds a certificate that does not certify the generated key. The client gets systemFailure and a CertificateConfirmer hears ConfirmRejected.

docs.title: Delayed issuance
docs.text: The key pair is generated when the request arrives. A waiting request keeps the encrypted private key until the CA decides. The client gets it with the certificate when it polls. Snapshots from SnapshotTransactions carry the encrypted key of every waiting request.

docs.title: Protocol version
docs.text: EnvelopedData is CMP version 3 syntax, so the response is version 3. OpenSSL clients send these requests as version 2 and read the version 3 answer.

docs.title: Delayed issuance and confirmation
docs.text: A CA does not have to decide at once. It can hold a request until an operator approves it or an HSM queue drains and it can learn whether the client accepted the certificate it issued.

docs.title: Waiting for a decision
docs.text:
Implement server.PendingChecker and return a WaitingResponse from IssueCertificate:

func (c *myCA) IssueCertificate(ctx context.Context, reqType server.RequestType,
    tmpl *x509.Certificate, sender *server.SenderIdentity) (*server.Response, error) {

    jobID := c.queue.Add(tmpl, sender)
    return &server.Response{Waiting: &server.WaitingResponse{
        CheckAfter: 30 * time.Second,
        Reason:     "waiting for operator approval",
        PollRef:    jobID,
    }}, nil
}

func (c *myCA) CheckPending(ctx context.Context, pollRef string,
    sender *server.SenderIdentity) (*server.Response, error) {

    switch job := c.queue.Get(pollRef); {
    case job.Pending():
        return &server.Response{Waiting: &server.WaitingResponse{CheckAfter: 30 * time.Second, PollRef: pollRef}}, nil
    case job.Rejected():
        return nil, &server.Error{Status: pkicmp.StatusRejection, FailureInfo: pkicmp.FailNotAuthorized}
    default:
        return &server.Response{Certificate: job.Certificate()}, nil
    }
}

The flow follows RFC 9483 section 4.4:

  1. The server answers the request with status waiting. Reason becomes its statusString.
  2. The client polls with pollReq after CheckAfter.
  3. The server calls CheckPending with the stored PollRef.
  4. CheckPending returns the certificate, another WaitingResponse or a *server.Error.

A rejection reaches the client in the ip, cp or kup it would have got at once, with the request's certReqId and ends the transaction. The final response grants implicit confirmation only when the delayed request asked for it.

docs.title: Polling rules
docs.text:
• pollRep advertises CheckAfter in whole seconds, at least one. A pollReq that arrives earlier gets another pollRep with the time left and does not reach the CA.
  • A pollReq names the request by its certReqId or by -1 for the whole message. A p10cr may also be polled with 0. Any other value is refused with badRequest.
  • A pollReq must repeat the senderNonce of the previous response in its recipNonce. WithOptionalPollReqRecipNonce accepts one without it, which the Insta Certifier clients need.

docs.title: Clients that stop polling
docs.text:
A request waits until CleanupExpired removes it, 24 hours after its last message by default. Set the lifetime with WithWaitingLifetime. It must exceed the CheckAfter you return. A CA that implements WaitingExpirer is told the PollRef of each request it loses this way, so it can close its own record.

How long a request may wait for a decision is your policy: CheckPending rejects a request you no longer want to decide.

The waiting state lives in the server. Replicas share it only through snapshots.

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
After an issued certificate, the client sends certConf to accept or reject it and the server answers pkiConf. Implement server.CertificateConfirmer to hear the outcome:

func (c *myCA) ConfirmCertificate(ctx context.Context, cert *x509.Certificate,
    status server.ConfirmStatus, issueRef any) error {

    switch status {
    case server.ConfirmAccepted, server.ConfirmImplicit:
        return c.store.Publish(issueRef)
    case server.ConfirmRejected, server.ConfirmExpired:
        return c.store.Revoke(issueRef)
    }
    return nil
}
Status Meaning ConfirmAccepted The client accepted the certificate ConfirmRejected The client rejected it or sent a certConf without any CertStatus ConfirmImplicit Implicit confirmation was granted, so no certConf follows ConfirmExpired No certConf arrived before the confirmation wait ended

issueRef is the Response.IssueRef you set in IssueCertificate, such as a database row ID.

WithConfirmWaitTime sets how long the server waits for certConf, 10 seconds by default. The value is sent to the client in the response.

docs.title: Rules for certConf
docs.text:
• Every CertStatus must carry the certHash and certReqId of the issued certificate. All of them must accept it or all must reject it. The CA is notified once.
  • For a p10cr the certReqId may be -1 or 0, because RFC 9810 and RFC 9483 disagree and deployed peers use both.
  • certConf must repeat the senderNonce of the certificate response in its recipNonce. WithOptionalCertConfRecipNonce accepts one without it. A different value is always refused.
  • certConf must use the credentials of the request, because the transaction is found by them. A key update that keeps its key is confirmed with the old certificate.

docs.title: Implicit confirmation
docs.text: WithImplicitConfirm grants implicit confirmation in every successful certificate response to a client that asks for it. The certificate then counts as confirmed and the certConf round trip is skipped. A certificate encrypted for proof by decryption never gets implicit confirmation, because its certConf is the proof. See Keys that cannot sign.

docs.title: Context values
docs.text:
A custom Handler built with server.New sees polls and confirmations as calls whose context carries these values. The CA callbacks get the same details as arguments.

Function Set while the server handles server.PollRefFromContext A poll for a delayed request server.IssueRefFromContext A certConf, with the IssueRef of the certificate server.IssuedCertFromContext A certConf, with the certificate being confirmed server.POPMethodFromContext A certificate request and its confirmation, with the proof of possession method

docs.title: Keys that cannot sign
docs.text:
By default only a signature proves possession of a key, so the server refuses a CRMF request for a key that cannot sign, such as ML-KEM. Two options accept proof by decryption (RFC 9810 section 5.2.8.3) for RSA, elliptic curve (ECDH) and ML-KEM keys:

Option Method When possession is proven WithEncryptedCertificatePOP The server returns the certificate encrypted for the requested key. The client proves possession by sending certConf with the hash of the decrypted certificate After the certificate is issued WithChallengeResponsePOP The server first sends a popdecc with a random number encrypted for the key. A popdecr with that number continues the request Before the request reaches your CA

Both are off by default. A key the server cannot encrypt for, such as X25519, is refused with badAlg. server.POPMethodFromContext tells your CA which method a request used.

docs.title: Encrypted certificate
docs.text:
The certificate exists before the client has proved anything, so treat it as undelivered until a matching certConf arrives:

  • Publish the certificate only after ConfirmAccepted.
  • Revoke it on ConfirmExpired or ConfirmRejected (RFC 9810 sections 5.2.8.3.2 and 8.11).

Such a request never gets implicit confirmation. A certConf with the wrong hash is refused with badPOP and leaves the transaction open until a matching one arrives or the confirmation wait ends. Implement CertificateConfirmer to hear the outcome, see Delayed issuance and confirmation.

docs.title: Challenge-response
docs.text: A wrong answer ends the transaction with badPOP and the certificate is never created. The challenge waits for its answer as long as an issued certificate waits for certConf, see WithConfirmWaitTime. Your CA sees the request only after the right answer, as if it had just arrived.

docs.title: Certifying an ML-KEM key
docs.text: crypto/x509 cannot certify an ML-KEM key, so the CA needs another way to sign such a certificate. The template carries the key as *mlkem.EncapsulationKey768 or *mlkem.EncapsulationKey1024. pkicmp.MarshalPublicKey encodes its SubjectPublicKeyInfo (RFC 9935), whose only allowed key usage is keyEncipherment.

docs.title: Response format
docs.text:
The encrypted certificate travels in CMS EnvelopedData, which is CMP version 3 syntax, so the response is version 3. One case differs:

Request Response Version 3, any key EnvelopedData in a version 3 response Version 2, ML-KEM or elliptic curve key EnvelopedData in a version 3 response Version 2, RSA key EncryptedValue in a version 2 response Version 2, RSA key, with WithEnvelopedDataForVersion2 EnvelopedData in a version 3 response

Version 2 RSA requests get the older EncryptedValue because OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.2 clients cannot read EnvelopedData. Other keys have no EncryptedValue form.

A Bouncy Castle client built on its CertificateResponse class reads only EnvelopedData. It must send version 3 for an RSA key, as RFC 9810 section 7 asks of a client that expects version 3 syntax. Set WithEnvelopedDataForVersion2 when your version 2 clients read only EnvelopedData. OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.2 clients then cannot read the certificate.

docs.title: Profile restrictions
docs.text: RFC 9483 section 4.1.1 requires a signature proof for a key that can sign. Under WithStrictProfileValidation only an ML-KEM key may use either method.

docs.title: Policy and client compatibility
docs.text: The server authenticates every message, but it does not decide who may request which certificate. That is the job of the policy middleware you pass to NewCAServer. Without a policy, any authenticated client could request any certificate for any name.

docs.title: Lightweight CMP Profile
docs.text:
server.LightweightPolicy() enforces the RFC 9483 rules a server needs:

  • A CRMF request proves possession of its key.
  • A key update is signature-protected.
  • A MAC-protected message identifies its secret through the sender name or senderKID.
  • A certificate template names the entity in its subject or in a requested subjectAltName with a NULL-DN subject (RFC 9483 section 4.1.1).
  • A request for a CA certificate is refused and BasicConstraints path lengths are validated.
  • A revocation request is signature-protected and carries a reasonCode.

Two checks run with or without a policy, because they establish what a request is rather than whether you grant it: proof of possession and the decoding of BasicConstraints.

docs.title: Your own authorization
docs.text:
A middleware wraps a server.Handler. Chain yours with MiddlewareChain. The first one runs first:

srv := server.NewCAServer(ca,
    server.MiddlewareChain(auditLog(logger), myPolicy(), server.LightweightPolicy()),
    server.WithSigner(caKey, caCert),
    server.WithSecretLookup(secrets),
    server.WithCertificateLookup(certs),
)

func myPolicy() func(server.Handler) server.Handler {
    return func(next server.Handler) server.Handler {
        return server.HandlerFunc(func(
            ctx context.Context, msg *pkicmp.PKIMessage, sender *server.SenderIdentity,
        ) (*server.Response, error) {
            if !isAllowed(sender) {
                return nil, &server.Error{
                    Status:      pkicmp.StatusRejection,
                    FailureInfo: pkicmp.FailNotAuthorized,
                    StatusText:  "not authorized",
                }
            }
            return next.HandleCMP(ctx, msg, sender)
        })
    }
}

Middleware is also the place for audit logging, metrics and rate limiting.

docs.title: Strict profile validation
docs.text:
Some RFC 9483 rules govern how a peer builds a message rather than how the server authenticates it. Deployed clients break them, so they are off by default. WithStrictProfileValidation turns them on:

  • A MAC-protected message must name its secret in a directoryName sender.
  • A signed request must carry extraCerts that lead with the protection certificate and form a chain.
  • A request must carry a transaction ID and every message a senderNonce of at least 128 bits.
  • A certConf must hold one CertStatus.
  • A certConf, pollReq or popdecr must not repeat the senderNonce of the last request or response in the transaction.
  • A signature proof of possession must not carry poposkInput.
  • Proof by decryption is allowed only for keys that cannot sign.

It also overrides every option in the table below except WithSHA1Signatures. Use it for a conformance test suite or a fleet known to follow RFC 9483 exactly. The Siemens CMP test suite runs against the server with it.

docs.title: Message time
docs.text: WithMessageTimeTolerance refuses a messageTime further than the tolerance from server time with badTime (RFC 9483 section 3.5). It is off by default because no single tolerance suits every deployment. A message without messageTime is not refused.

docs.title: Options for deployed clients
docs.text:
Each option relaxes one rule for clients that break it. The server still checks everything that authenticates the request.

Option Accepts Needed by WithOptionalCertConfRecipNonce A certConf without recipNonce Clients that leave the field out WithOptionalPollReqRecipNonce A pollReq without recipNonce Insta Certifier 10 cmpclient and Insta Certifier 7 ssh-cmpclient, to collect a delayed result WithPoposkInputVariants A signature proof that carries poposkInput although the template holds subject and key Insta Certifier 10 cmpclient WithSignatureProtectionPOP A CRMF request without proof whose protection was signed with the requested key Insta Certifier 7 ssh-cmpclient UPDATE that keeps the key WithOptionalSubject A template without the subject field that names the entity in subjectAltName Clients that leave the field out WithAnyCertReqID An ir, cr or kur with a certReqId other than 0, repeated in the response RFC 4210 clients that number their requests, tests of the certReqId check of a client WithOptionalRevocationReason A revocation request without reasonCode Insta Certifier 10 cmpclient rr WithOptionalRevocationIssuer A revocation request without an issuer Clients that name only the serial number WithMACRevocation A MAC-protected revocation request, decided by RevocationAuthorizer Clients that revoke with a shared secret WithSHA1Signatures SHA-1 signatures in protection and proof of possession RFC 4210 era devices

Server options describes each option in full and Tested implementations lists which client needs which option. A refused request names its rule in the status text, and Troubleshooting maps that text to the option.

docs.title: RFC 4210 clients
docs.text: Clients that implement only RFC 4210 work with the defaults. The server assigns a transaction ID to a first request without one, accepts a shorter senderNonce and accepts the MAC from a NULL-DN sender with senderKID. The SHA-1 PasswordBasedMac suite such clients often use is accepted and the response repeats it.

docs.title: Registration authorities
docs.text:
A registration authority (RA) can approve a request by forwarding it unchanged inside a nested message that carries the RA's own protection (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.1). Accept such messages with WithRAAuthorizer:

server.WithRAAuthorizer(server.RAAuthorizerFunc(func(ctx context.Context,
    ra *server.SenderIdentity, req *pkicmp.PKIMessage, sender *server.SenderIdentity) error {

    if ra.Certificate == nil || !ra.Certificate.Equal(raCert) {
        return &server.Error{Status: pkicmp.StatusRejection, FailureInfo: pkicmp.FailNotAuthorized}
    }
    return nil
}))

Without an authorizer, nested messages are refused with badRequest.

docs.title: How a forwarded request is handled
docs.text:
1. The server verifies the protection of the nested message with SecretLookup or CertificateLookup.
  2. It verifies the protection of the forwarded request the same way.
  3. It calls the authorizer with both identities.
  4. It handles the request as if the end entity had sent it directly. SenderIdentity.RA tells your CA which RA approved it.

The response is protected for the end entity, uses its protocol version and is not wrapped in a nested message. Problems with the nested message itself, including a refusal by the authorizer, are reported to the RA in an error message.

The authorizer runs for every forwarded message, including certConf and pollReq.

docs.title: Identify the RA
docs.text:
A verified protection proves only who sent a message. Every end entity with a certificate or shared secret can produce a valid nested message, so the authorizer must identify the RA itself, for example by comparing ra.Certificate with the RA certificates you trust.

RFC 9483 requires the RA to sign the nested message, while RFC 4210 also allows a MAC. ra.MACVerified reports a MAC. Refuse it with wrongIntegrity to follow the Lightweight CMP Profile. The example above refuses a MAC, because ra.Certificate is nil for one.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• The nested message must copy the transaction ID and senderNonce of the request it wraps.
  • One nested message carries one request. Batches of several messages (RFC 9483 section 5.2.2.2) are refused with badRequest.

A go-pki-cmp client acts as the RA with client.WithRegistrationAuthority, see Acting as a registration authority.

An RA that revokes on behalf of end entities signs the rr with its own certificate. That is handled by RevocationAuthorizer, see Revocation.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
Implement server.Revoker to accept revocation requests (RFC 9483 section 4.2). Without it the server refuses every rr with badRequest.

func (c *myCA) RevokeCertificate(ctx context.Context, req *server.RevocationRequest,
    sender *server.SenderIdentity) error {

    cert := c.store.Find(req.Issuer, req.SerialNumber)
    if err := req.Match(cert); err != nil {
        return err // badCertId
    }
    if c.store.IsRevoked(cert) {
        return &server.Error{Status: pkicmp.StatusRejection, FailureInfo: pkicmp.FailCertRevoked}
    }
    return c.store.Revoke(cert, req.Reason)
}

The CA must find the certificate itself and report, as RFC 9483 section 5.1.3 asks:

  • badCertId when it did not issue the certificate. RevocationRequest.Match also checks the optional template fields against the certificate found.
  • certRevoked when the certificate is already revoked.

A nil error reports the revocation as accepted in the rp. pkicmp.CRLReasonRemoveFromCRL asks to release a certificate from hold.

RevocationRequest.InvalidityDate is the invalidityDate the request asks for (RFC 5280 section 5.3.2), the time at which the key was compromised or the certificate otherwise became invalid, for the CA to publish in the CRL entry. It is zero when the request carries none. A request whose invalidityDate is not a GeneralizedTime is refused with badDataFormat and one that carries two with badRequest. Extensions holds every requested CRL entry extension for the CA to read.

docs.title: Who may revoke
docs.text:
The server authorizes the request before it calls RevokeCertificate. By default only the certificate being revoked may sign the request, as RFC 9483 section 4.2 requires. A request signed by anyone else, such as a registration authority (RFC 9483 section 5.3.2), is refused with notAuthorized unless the CA implements server.RevocationAuthorizer and approves it:

func (c *myCA) AuthorizeRevocation(ctx context.Context, req *server.RevocationRequest,
    sender *server.SenderIdentity) error {

    if sender.Certificate != nil && c.isRA(sender.Certificate) {
        return nil
    }
    return &server.Error{Status: pkicmp.StatusRejection, FailureInfo: pkicmp.FailNotAuthorized}
}

LightweightPolicy refuses MAC-protected revocation requests with wrongIntegrity. WithMACRevocation passes them on and they always go to RevocationAuthorizer. A shared secret proves who holds the secret, not who holds the certificate, so decide which certificates that secret may revoke, for example only those it enrolled.

docs.title: Missing fields
docs.text: Option Accepts WithOptionalRevocationReason A request without reasonCode. It reaches the CA with reason unspecified, which RFC 5280 treats the same way WithOptionalRevocationIssuer A request that names only a serial number. A request signed with that certificate revokes the signer's own certificate and the server fills in the issuer. Any other request reaches RevocationAuthorizer with an empty RawIssuer and the CA must refuse it when several issuers use that serial number

docs.title: Delayed revocation
docs.text: RevokeCertificate or AuthorizeRevocation can return a *server.WaitingError when the decision has to wait, for example for an operator. The client gets an error message with status waiting and polls with certReqId -1. Each poll reaches PendingChecker.CheckPending with the PollRef. A nil Response from CheckPending means the revocation is done and the client receives the rp. See Delayed issuance and confirmation.

docs.title: Support messages
docs.text:
RFC 9483 section 4.3 defines general messages that ask the CA for information. Implement the matching provider to answer each one:

Interface Request RFC CACertificatesProvider Intermediate and issuing CA certificates RFC 9483 section 4.3.1 RootCAUpdateProvider An update of the root CA certificate RFC 9483 section 4.3.2 CertReqTemplateProvider A certificate request template, per certificate profile RFC 9483 section 4.3.3 CRLProvider A CRL update or the current CRL RFC 9483 section 4.3.4, RFC 9810 section 5.3.19.6

The server answers a genm with a genp and lists every requested type without a provider in an unsupportedOIDs item (RFC 9810 section 5.3.19.7). The client then knows that the CA does not offer the type, rather than reading an absent value as "no update".

func (c *myCA) LatestCRL(ctx context.Context, source pkicmp.CRLSource,
    sender *server.SenderIdentity) (*x509.RevocationList, error) {

    // A zero source asks for the current CRL of the CA's choice.
    if !source.IsZero() && !slices.ContainsFunc(source.DirectoryNames(), c.issues) {
        return nil, nil // no CRL from this source
    }
    return c.store.LatestCRL()
}

Return nil when the CA has nothing to send. The response then carries an absent value.

docs.title: Rules the server enforces
docs.text:
• A root CA update must carry newWithOld, the new root certified by the old one. The server checks it with pkicmp.RootCAKeyUpdate.Verify before sending it and answers systemFailure when it fails.
  • A CRL update is sent only when the CRL is newer than the thisUpdate the client reported.
  • A general message completes its transaction at once and is never delayed. A custom Handler answers with Response.GeneralResponse and gets systemFailure if it returns a WaitingResponse.
  • WithStrictProfileValidation requires one item per request and an absent value where RFC 9483 defines none.

The example CA implements every provider. Its root never changes, so it reports no root CA update.

docs.title: Transactions and recovery
docs.text: The server tracks multi-message exchanges such as ir, ip, certConf and pkiConf and the polling flows. This page covers the limits, the cleanup and moving the state to durable storage.

docs.title: Transaction identity
docs.text: Transactions are keyed by the sender's verified credential and the transaction ID, so one client cannot continue another client's transaction (RFC 9810 section 5.1.1). For a MAC-protected client the credential is the shared secret itself, whichever header field selected it, and for a signed client it is the protection certificate. A client may leave the transaction ID out of its first request. The server then assigns a random 128-bit one and returns it, as RFC 4210 and RFC 9810 require. WithStrictProfileValidation refuses such requests instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Option Default Effect WithMaxTransactions 10000 Concurrent transactions in the server WithMaxTransactionsPerCredential 100 Concurrent transactions per client credential WithConfirmWaitTime 10 seconds How long an issued certificate or a challenge waits for its answer WithWaitingLifetime 24 hours How long a waiting request stays after the client's last poll server.MaxRequestBodySize 1 MiB Largest accepted request body

A new request beyond a transaction limit is refused with systemUnavail. A first message that reuses the transaction ID of a transaction the server still holds is refused with transactionIdInUse, also when the limits are full.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Call CleanupExpired periodically. It removes completed and stale transactions, tells CertificateConfirmer about certificates that were never confirmed and tells WaitingExpirer about requests whose client stopped polling:

go func() {
    for range time.Tick(time.Minute) {
        srv.CleanupExpired()
    }
}()

Entries expire by last activity: WithConfirmWaitTime for most, WithWaitingLifetime for waiting requests. A certConf that arrives after the confirmWaitTime is refused with badRequest even before CleanupExpired runs. CertificateConfirmer then hears ConfirmExpired, as RFC 9483 section 4.1.1 asks.

docs.title: Durable recovery
docs.text:
SnapshotTransactions saves the active, waiting, issued and completed protocol state. RestoreTransactions loads it into a fresh server with the same response-signing certificate before that server accepts requests. Original nonces, credential binding, timestamps and MAC parameters survive.

The host must:

  • Exclude concurrent ServeHTTP, CleanupExpired, snapshot and restore calls.
  • Persist a successful response and its snapshot before sending that response to the peer.
  • Commit issuance records and credential usage in the same durable operation.
  • Keep a response cache when exact request retries must not issue another certificate or reuse a completed transaction ID. The library provides neither database transactions nor a response cache.

Treat snapshots as trusted private server data, never as client input. They have a versioned format and contain no secrets or signing keys, unless your IssueRef holds them. A waiting request for central key generation keeps its private key encrypted for the client. IssueRef must be JSON serializable. Pass a decoder to RestoreTransactions when its original Go type matters. A nil decoder uses the standard encoding/json value types.

Restore refuses a different signer, invalid state and capacity overruns without replacing existing state. Snapshots are limited to 64 MiB. Expiration timestamps are preserved, so keep calling CleanupExpired after a restore.

docs.title: Several replicas
docs.text: The state lives in one process. Replicas behind one endpoint share it only through snapshots, so either route every message of a transaction to the same replica or restore the state before a replica serves the next message.
